lead: Sixteen videos, four angles, one answer: the splash feels like a game because it is ONE world with a character in it; the next screens feel like UI because they cut to a form. Keep the student inside the floating town from the first frame to the map, let Wael ask every question and react to every tap, make each choice an object in that world, move the camera instead of swapping pages, and juice the one thing the student actually does — answering.

principles.title: 1. One world, no page cuts
principles.detail: Every step happens in the same place: the island stays on screen, the camera pans or zooms, and only the content that changes moves. Direction of motion is a promise about the map of the app, so keep it consistent (forward = one side, back = the other).

principles.title: 2. Choices are objects in the world — but as fast as a button
principles.detail: Level and subject become things in the town (floors, signposts, the subject's building) that light up, react and are picked in one tap with a big Arabic label. In-world UI must never be slower or less readable than the flat version, or it breaks the immersion it was meant to create.

principles.title: 3. Wael is the voice of every step and reacts to every tap
principles.detail: The best onboardings are a conversation with a character: he asks the question, and each answer gets an immediate, personal reaction (pose + one line). Like the paddle with eyes in Juice it or lose it, a character that looks at what you touch turns a UI element into someone.

principles.title: 4. Play before asking — the account protects what was earned
principles.detail: Willingness to learn grows with investment. Give a real first win within the first minutes, then frame sign-up as 'don't lose your progress', one field per screen, permissions only after the win with a primer in Wael's voice.

principles.title: 5. One decision per screen, with a recommended default
principles.detail: Working memory has few slots. Each screen asks one thing, shows 3–5 large labelled options, pre-highlights the likely one (Wael gesturing at it) so the choice becomes 'accept or change', and every answer shrinks what comes next (pick Bac → only Bac subjects). One obvious big call to action per screen is the golden path.

principles.title: 6. Teach by doing: the first question IS the tutorial
principles.detail: No 'tap here' arrows (people follow them without learning). The first question is a gate that teaches the tap itself, safe to fail, then one new nuance per question. Show, don't tell: short looping demos and familiar icons beat text.

principles.title: 7. Juice the core verb, and dose it
principles.detail: Answering must feel good even in an empty room: press squash, a sound on the same frame, a particle puff, a tiny hit-stop on a correct answer, the pitch rising over a streak of right answers. Stack many small effects; keep the loudest ones (burst, shake, Wael cheering) for correct answers and the result.

principles.title: 8. Progress lives in the world, and stays
principles.detail: Replace the app progress bar with in-world progress (path stones or lanterns lighting up on the island). Leave traces of what the student did (the chosen subject's building lit, the 3 answers as stamps) instead of wiping each screen. Vague, felt progress beats exact numbers early on.

principles.title: 9. Never punish; help invisibly
principles.detail: A wrong answer is a soft catch (Wael shows the right one, the student continues), never a red fail screen. When a student struggles, quietly lower the pressure; visible or mocking help ('easy mode') hurts pride and immersion. Design the mistake path to delight.

principles.title: 10. No dead frames — and no slow gimmicks
principles.detail: Something is always alive on screen (Wael idles, a 'Wael prépare ton défi' beat instead of a blank load). But cinematic in-world moments must be short, interruptible and shorter on repeat runs.

flow.title: Splash — the door
flow.detail: Already right: one world, Wael in it, one lime CTA. On tap the island does NOT disappear: the camera starts its move and Wael walks with it into the next step.

flow.title: Welcome — 'Hi, I'm Wael, 3 quick steps then we play'
flow.detail: Wael introduces himself in a dialogue box at the bottom, names a short finite number of steps and promises the game as the payoff. The island stays behind him; the 3 steps appear as 3 path stones on the island, not as white cards.

flow.title: Level — floors or signposts, Bac pre-highlighted
flow.detail: The camera moves to the school; the levels are its floors (1ère → Bac) or signposts, big labels, the likely one glowing with Wael gesturing at it. One tap: Wael nods, a stone lights up on the path, the camera moves on.

flow.title: Subject — tap the building
flow.detail: Only that level's subjects: each is its building on the island (maths tower, lab, library, greenhouse…), labelled in Arabic. Tapping one lights it, Wael turns to it, and the building grows into the game header (container transform).

flow.title: The 3 questions — inside the building
flow.detail: Question 1 teaches the tap (obvious answer, instant feedback, zero penalty). Answers are chunky pressable cards with full juice; right = burst + rising pitch + Wael cheers; wrong = soft catch with the right answer shown. Difficulty of questions 2–3 adapts quietly.

flow.title: Result — a celebration you own
flow.detail: The 3 answers stay as stamps, points fly onto the island and the subject's building visibly levels up. One big burst, Wael celebrates on the same frame.

flow.title: Account — 'don't lose your town'
flow.detail: Asked only now, framed as saving what was built, one field per screen in a sheet over the town, Google/Apple first; notifications asked after, with a primer in Wael's voice.

flow.title: The town — revealed, not dumped
flow.detail: First arrival: one lit building (the one just played), the rest dimmed; HUD counters appear one at a time as they become meaningful; every building has a short Arabic label.

transitions.title: Steps = shared axis, RTL-aware
transitions.detail: welcome → level → subject → questions slide together along one horizontal axis with a crossfade, ~300 ms. In Arabic, forward brings the new step from the LEFT; Back plays the exact reverse.

transitions.title: Persistent layers never pop
transitions.detail: The island backdrop, Wael and the progress path get their own transition layer (view-transition-name): they stay or glide to their new size and position while only the step content moves.

transitions.title: The chosen thing becomes the next screen
transitions.detail: Container transform: the tapped subject building/badge grows into the game header; the result card grows into the account sheet. The eye never loses the object.

transitions.title: Springs, not curves
transitions.detail: Duration first, then bounce: 0 for camera and panels, ~0.15 for chips, ~0.25–0.3 for Wael and the result pop, never above ~0.4. Springs are interruptible: a second tap redirects instead of jolting.

transitions.title: Choreography
transitions.detail: Ease-out for entrances, ease-in for exits; overlap group entrances (each starts ~40 ms after the previous, before it finishes); animate similar things the same way; match speeds, not durations. Write each transition as a 300 ms timeline (background over the full span, scrim in the first third, new content in a short middle window).

transitions.title: Overlays bloom, they don't travel
transitions.detail: Dialogs, hints and the result card: quick fade + scale up from ~0.92, plain faster fade out. Use fade-through only where two steps have no spatial link.

transitions.title: Reduced motion and repeat runs
transitions.detail: prefers-reduced-motion → a short crossfade instead of slides and camera moves ('reduced' is not 'none'). Second and later runs: shorter or skippable cinematics.

avoid.title: Hard page cuts ('click, pop')
avoid.detail: They throw away the context of where things came from — the single biggest reason the flow reads as UI.

avoid.title: White cards in a grid + a boxed character
avoid.detail: That is the grey Breakout baseline: correct, playable and lifeless. The character belongs in the scene, not in a side panel.

avoid.title: 'Tap here' arrows and decoy controls
avoid.detail: Arrows teach nothing; a fake button next to the real one makes people tap and fail.

avoid.title: Unlabelled or misleading icons
avoid.detail: An hourglass 'end turn' stuck a playtester for 40 minutes; bare icons make people guess. Short labels always.

avoid.title: Slow in-world gimmicks
avoid.detail: A clever long animation is charming once and tiresome forever.

avoid.title: Fail screens and mocking help
avoid.detail: Red 'wrong' walls, 'easy mode' labels or silly penalties for needing help break pride and flow.

avoid.title: Everything loud, everything 200 ms
avoid.detail: Motion has the loudest voice; if every element shouts nothing stands out, and one blanket duration makes related objects stop looking related.
